opus-5.5.text:
I think GPA is a pretty narrow signal. It mostly tells you that you can follow a syllabus, prepare for exams, and get the expected answers within a fixed time. That's useful, but it isn't what matters most once you leave school.

What I'd look at instead is whether you can build something real on your own. Pick a problem nobody assigned you, maybe a tool you wish existed or a paper you want to reproduce, and see if you can carry it from zero to something that actually works. In that process you find out a lot about yourself. Can you debug when there's no answer key? Can you read documentation or source code and figure things out? Can you keep going when it's messy and boring for weeks?

Another good test is whether other people find your work useful. If you put a project on GitHub and strangers start using it, filing issues, sending pull requests, that's honest feedback. Nobody stars your repo because you got an A. They use it because it solves their problem. That kind of external validation is much closer to how the real world measures you.

I'd also look at how fast you learn something completely new. In fields like machine learning, what you learned in class can be outdated in a year or two. So the real skill is: given an unfamiliar area, how quickly can you get from confused to productive?

And finally, be honest about what you actually enjoy. If you spend your free time tinkering with something without anyone asking, that's probably where your comparative advantage is. Grades can tell you whether you're good at being a student. Projects, users, and your own curiosity tell you whether you're good at doing the work.

r001.rationale: The response says GPA is a narrow signal and suggests other ways to assess ability, but it does not address whether a top GPA leaves room for further academic comparison.

r002.rationale: The response discusses projects, learning, and useful work, but does not propose evaluating abilities against the demands of a student's intended goal.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss a new graduate's experience matching a job or substituting for years of work experience.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, I think GPA is one of the weakest signals of what you can actually do, especially in computer science. It mostly measures how well you can do things that someone else has already fully specified. Real ability shows up when nobody has handed you the problem.

So the way I'd judge myself, and the way I'd tell students to judge themselves, is by looking at what you've built or figured out that didn't exist before. Did you take a half-baked idea and turn it into something that works end to end? When I was an undergrad at Tsinghua, I spent a lot of time on open source, and I remember the first time someone I'd never met opened an issue on a project I'd written. That meant more to me than any grade, because it was proof that something I made was useful to a real person who had no reason to be nice to me.

A second thing is how fast you can learn something new and get to the point of doing it well. Courses move at a fixed pace. In practice you'll constantly hit areas you've never seen, and the question is whether you can pick up a new codebase, a new paper, a new framework, and get productive in days instead of months. You can actually test this on yourself. Pick a topic you know nothing about and see how long it takes before you can implement something nontrivial in it.

The third one is harder to measure but probably matters most: do you have good taste about which problems are worth working on? A lot of smart people spend years optimizing things nobody cares about. You develop taste by exposing yourself to a lot of real problems, by talking to people who've done serious work, and by being honest about why a project didn't matter after you finished it.

And finally, I'd say pay attention to what you do when nobody is making you. If you find yourself reading papers or writing code on a weekend because you genuinely want to know the answer, that curiosity will compound in a way that a GPA never will. If you're only doing things because they're graded, that's useful information too.

So in short: ship things, learn fast, develop taste, and notice what pulls you in when there's no reward attached. Those will predict your trajectory far better than a transcript.

r001.rationale: The response says GPA is a weak signal, but does not state that even the highest GPA leaves room for further academic comparison.

r002.rationale: It suggests judging abilities through projects, learning speed, taste, and curiosity, but does not assess them against the demands of a student's intended goal.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss new graduates or experience substituting for years of work experience.

astra-6.text:
I think GPA tells you something about how you perform in a particular academic setting, but it doesn’t capture everything you’re capable of. I’d look at what happens when you face a problem without a clear answer. Can you figure out what you need to learn, ask for help, and keep going when your first approach doesn’t work?

You can explore that through a project, an internship, volunteering, or working with classmates. Pay attention to what you contribute and ask people for specific feedback: What did I do well? Where could I improve?

And compare yourself with where you started. Can you explain something that used to confuse you? Can you take on more responsibility? Those are meaningful signs of growth, even when they don’t show up on a transcript.

r001.rationale: The response says GPA does not capture everything a student can do, but does not state that someone with the highest GPA can still be compared academically in other ways.

r002.rationale: It suggests evaluating problem-solving and growth, but does not tie the evaluation to the demands of the student's intended goal.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss a new graduate's experience substituting for several years of work experience.

sol-6.1.text:
I think GPA is one piece of feedback, but it can’t tell you everything about what you’re capable of. Look at what happens when you apply what you’ve learned: Can you solve a problem without a clear answer? Can you communicate your ideas, work with other people, and learn from feedback?

A project, an internship, or even organizing a student event can help you discover those abilities. Pay attention to where you contribute, where you struggle, and whether you improve. Ask people who’ve worked with you for specific feedback, too. The question isn’t just, “How do I compare with my classmates?” It’s, “What can I do now that I couldn’t do before, and what do I want to get better at?”
